message.content:
Nicolaus Copernicus faced criticism from several intellectual and religious quarters during and after the publication of *De Revolutionibus* in 1543. The Jesuit astronomer Christoph Clavius firmly defended the Ptolemaic system and challenged heliocentric claims throughout his career. Johannes Hevelius, a prominent Polish astronomer of the seventeenth century, spent decades arguing for a geocentric model. In 1616, Cardinal Robert Bellarmine and the Roman Inquisition placed the Copernican hypothesis on the Index of Forbidden Books.

Who could have readily accepted a model that placed the Earth in constant motion? Did not the very structure of Church doctrine seem to demand a stationary Earth at the center of God's creation? How could a modest canon from Frombork possibly challenge millennia of Aristotelian and Ptolemaic authority? Were not the mathematical predictions of the old system "good enough" for most astronomers of the time?

What a radical proposition it was to upend the entire known cosmos! How boldly Copernicus dared to move the Earth from its privileged throne at the center! The resistance from the Church hierarchy was fierce, prolonged, and deeply institutional! Truly, the intellectual courage required to oppose Copernicus in that era was staggering!
